questions.q: What is the expected number of fair-coin flips needed to see two heads in a row (HH)?
questions.explain: Using a two-state expectation setup (last flip tails vs. last flip heads) and solving the resulting equations gives E0 = 6, confirmed by simulation.

questions.q: In the Bayes' theorem example (1% disease prevalence, 95% sensitivity, 90% specificity), why is the probability of actually having the disease given a positive test only about 8.8%, despite the test's high sensitivity?
options: Because the test's sensitivity figure was misquoted
Because the low base rate (1% prevalence) means false positives from the much larger healthy population outnumber true positives
Because specificity has no effect on the calculation
Because Bayes' theorem only applies to independent events
questions.explain: With a 1% base rate, even a 10% false-positive rate among the 99% healthy population produces more false positives than true positives from the 1% with the disease, pulling the posterior down to about 8.8%.

questions.q: In the gambler's ruin problem with a fair coin, starting at $5 with absorbing barriers at $0 and $10, what is the probability of reaching $10 before $0?
options: 0.5, because for a fair random walk the probability equals the starting position divided by the total range (k/N)
1.0, because a fair coin guarantees eventual success
0.1, because there are 10 total dollars at stake
It cannot be determined without knowing the number of rounds
questions.explain: For a symmetric (p=0.5) random walk between absorbing barriers 0 and N starting at k, the probability of reaching N first is exactly k/N — here 5/10 = 0.5.

questions.q: In the optimal-stopping (secretary) problem, what is the strategy and the resulting success probability for large N?
options: Accept the first candidate; success probability is 1/N
Reject the first N/e candidates as a benchmark, then accept the first candidate who beats all seen so far; success probability approaches 1/e ≈ 0.368
Interview all N candidates before deciding; success probability is 1.0
Randomly accept any candidate; success probability is 0.5
questions.explain: The optimal strategy rejects the first N/e candidates to set a benchmark, then accepts the next one who's the best seen so far, succeeding with probability approaching 1/e as N grows large.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what are interviewers in a math/probability round actually scoring?
options: Only whether the final numeric answer is correct
How quickly you can state a memorized formula
Whether you define the problem precisely, break it into manageable cases, sanity-check your answer, and keep reasoning out loud even when stuck
Whether you ask the interviewer to simply tell you the answer
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that clean, audible reasoning toward a wrong answer usually scores better than a correct answer with no shown work, since the interviewer is evaluating process.
